title: Will a Fiscal Miracle Happen in Colombia?
gist: Former Colombian finance minister Mauricio Cárdenas warns that Colombia faces its largest-ever fiscal deficit (7.8% of GDP in 2026, possibly over 9% in 2027) after Petro-era populism. He argues that De La Espriella's IMF-backed fiscal rescue bill, which relies on VAT and income-tax increases, is technically sound but lacks the votes, and that failure could trigger a market and economic crisis.

insights.claim: Colombia ended 2025 with a fiscal deficit of 6.4% of GDP and is projected to close 2026 at 7.8%. The independent Fiscal Rule Advisory Committee estimates the gap could exceed 9% of GDP in 2027 without more measures, which would be the largest in Colombia's history and in Latin America and the Caribbean.

insights.so_what: Colombia's sovereign credit is on track for the worst deficit in the region. That is a ratings and spread risk.

insights.claim: Petro's government cancelled its IMF Flexible Credit Line in October 2025, and the IMF withdrew from Colombia's fiscal debate. The author argues markets kept financing Petro without asking questions but charged a price for it.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: Without IMF oversight, discipline fell to markets through higher yields.

insights.claim: In September 2026, De La Espriella opened talks with the IMF. Some analysts estimate Colombia could get up to $16 billion in three annual installments from 2027, most likely through an Extended Fund Facility similar to Ecuador's.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: An IMF EFF would provide an external anchor and financing that could compress spreads.

insights.claim: The government's IMF-praised fiscal rescue bill aims to cut the 2027 deficit by 2.2 percentage points of GDP, mostly through taxes, and projects a deficit of 4% of GDP by 2030.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: The path to 4% by 2030 is the benchmark for judging Colombian fiscal credibility.
insights.locator: Praised by the IMF, the government

insights.claim: The bill would move coffee, fertilizers, private health insurance and other goods from reduced VAT rates (0% and 5%) to the standard 19%.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: Higher VAT on fertilizers and coffee raises input costs for agriculture and adds inflation pressure.

insights.claim: The bill would lower Colombia's personal income tax threshold from about $2,800 to $1,700 of monthly income, at a 9% marginal rate, affecting about three million workers.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: Broadening the tax base hits the middle class and is a key political hurdle.

insights.claim: Cárdenas calls the bill's proposals technically sound but politically radioactive, and judging from social media posts, including by pro-government lawmakers, he says the president does not have the votes to pass it.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: The low odds of passage in current form imply dilution risk that markets may be underpricing.

insights.claim: Cárdenas argues that voters do not want to hear about taxes until they see spending cuts, so the government should first make cuts that need no congressional approval.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: Executive-only cuts would be an early signal of credibility. Watch for them.

insights.claim: Cárdenas argues that eliminating fuel subsidies, which the government has been unwilling to do, is a key executive-only cut, alongside merging agencies, reducing staff, ending temporary contracts and setting a public-sector salary policy.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: A move on fuel subsidies would raise fuel prices and inflation in the short term but strongly improve fiscal credibility.

insights.claim: Unless De La Espriella builds legislative majorities and forms a coalition, the fiscal rescue bill risks failing or being heavily diluted, either of which would be a serious political setback.
insights.speaker: MAURICIO CÁRDENAS
insights.so_what: Coalition-building news in Congress is the leading indicator for Colombian assets.
